_note: The Health Passport P0 service's contract: what it stores, what its consent gateway refuses and in which words, what break-glass opens, and why it will not run anywhere but a developer's machine. apps/passport reads this file and types none of its sentences. It is not packages/catalog/passport.json, which is the fictional record the patient-facing Passport screens draw; this is the service that would one day hold a real one, and it is kept apart so that a screen fixture and a store's refusals cannot be edited as one thing.
_fiction: Every subject this service has ever held is a synthetic token it minted itself. No name, identity number, phone number or address is accepted into it, and nothing here was ever about a person.
_whyDevelopmentOnly: The master document says the Passport is live before the first visit only after its DPIA is signed. docs/PRIVACY-AND-SECURITY.md records that there is no DPIA, no registered Information Officer and no data residency decision, and that the keys here are an environment variable rather than an HSM or KMS. So the service refuses to start without an explicit development flag, binds to the loopback only, refuses a request whose Host is not a loopback name, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build if anything under deploy/ names it or its port.

service.why: Its own port, its own database file and its own key variable, each checked against the identity service's at start-up — the database by its real path, so a relative path, a symlink or the identity service's documented default cannot slip past a string comparison. An environment is development only when it names one of the development words, in any case; anything else, including Production and prod, is refused. The development flag is a phrase rather than true, so that nobody sets it by copying a line meant for something else. The Host header is held to a loopback name because a browser tricked by DNS rebinding connects from the loopback address with somebody else's hostname.

patientSession.why: A patient session here is a development stand-in for an OIDC login that does not exist, and it is a bearer token. It lives no longer than the identity service's own idle limit for a session — scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds the two to the same number — it can be ended, and a token with anything more than a payload and a signature is refused.

resources.why: A reference token and nothing else. Who the person is lives in the identity service.
Readings, filed under the category a reader is granted. Maternal health is protected in packages/catalog/records.json, so an observation filed there is sealed.
The first thing an emergency summary carries.

What the patient is taking. records.json has no category of its own for a medication statement, so it is filed under the prescription or the dispense it came from — a mapping to be settled when the record contract grows one.
The patient's own consent records, stored as FHIR Consent. The grants the gateway enforces are signed artefacts beside them, not rows anybody can edit.

Written by the gateway on every write, never by a caller, and encrypted under the same key as the entry it describes — a provenance saying 'HIV viral load at an antenatal visit' is as sealed as the reading.
Written by the gateway on every access, granted or refused, into a hash chain the patient can read.

identityScreen.why: Checked at every depth of every resource a caller writes, and on a break-glass note: a key that holds who somebody is, an extension whose url says it does, or a run of nine or more digits — a South African mobile number has ten and an identity number thirteen — or anything shaped like an email address. It cannot recognise a name written into free text, and nothing here claims it can; who performed an act is taken from the grant into the provenance, so a caller has no reason to write a performer at all.

sealed.why: A category packages/catalog/records.json marks protected is sealed: stored under a data key of its own, opened only by a grant whose sealed tick names that category in its scope, and never in the emergency summary. A tick that names no sealed category is refused, so a tick cannot quietly open something nobody named. An entry the patient marks private is sealed more tightly still, under its own key, and in P0 no grant opens it at all: there is not yet a way for a patient to release one private entry to one named grant, and until there is, a private entry is theirs alone.

emergencySummary.why: Allergies and current medicines — the part of the master document's default summary this store holds in P0. A grant opens the summary when its scope includes the emergency card; break-glass opens it and nothing else. Sealed and private entries are never in it, because P0 has no way for a patient to opt one in. A role that reads the emergency summary only may be granted exactly the items of its own default scope — for a responder, the emergency card and the trip's transport — and nothing more.

reasons.sentence: Break-glass: the patient is unresponsive and cannot consent.
Break-glass: the patient is conscious but has no phone or session with which to consent.
Break-glass: the patient cannot communicate a decision and no delegate can be reached.

breakGlass.why: When a patient cannot consent, a registered clinician or the dispatch desk may open the emergency summary only. Who they are comes from an operator credential, never from the request body; in P0 that credential is a development-only signed token minted at the console with node apps/passport/src/operator.ts, standing in for the OIDC login and mutual TLS that do not exist. They choose one of the listed reasons and write a note. The reason's sentence goes into the patient-visible audit chain. The note does not: it is screened for phone numbers, identity numbers and email addresses and refused if it carries one, and it is then stored encrypted under the patient's own key beside the audit entry, for the governance review within the window. The chain is kept for the life of the record and read by the patient, and free text a clinician wrote under pressure is exactly where a name and an address end up; keeping the note out of it means the most widely read log never holds what the screen cannot catch.

developerCredential.why: Creating a synthetic subject mints a patient session, so it is not open to whatever reaches the loopback. It needs a developer credential minted at the console with node apps/passport/src/operator.ts developer, from the same loaded configuration as the service, under a signing key of its own — a development-only stand-in, like the operator credential, for an authenticated person that does not exist yet. A working day long, so a credential left in a shell history does not outlive the session that used it.

statements.sealedExists: Sealed content exists in this record. The patient can release it, so ask them.
statements.breakGlassOpened: Opened by break-glass. This access is logged, the patient and their next of kin are told, and the governance board reviews it within {hours} hours.
statements.granted: Opened under a consent grant, for the purpose it names.
statements.patientSession: Opened by the patient in their own session.
statements.keys: Keys are envelope encryption under a master key held in an environment variable. That is not an HSM or a KMS, and nothing here claims it is.
statements.linkUsed: Opened through a share link the patient made, for the purpose its grant names, and counted against its uses.
statements.exported: The patient's own record, exported in their own session.
statements.hl7Received: Sent by a registered development partner as an HL7 v2 message, and matched to this record by a hospital number the patient linked.
statements.hl7Replayed: A registered development partner sent a message the Passport already had. The first acknowledgement was sent again, and nothing was written twice.
statements.identifierLinked: Linked by the patient in their own session. A message carrying this number may now be matched to this record, and to no other.
statements.quarantineRead: Read by a developer: which messages the Passport could not file and why, with nothing any of them said.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport service runs in development only, on synthetic data. It will not start without MYTHUSO_PASSPORT_DEVELOPMENT set to synthetic-data-only.
refusals.why: There is no DPIA, no Information Officer and no residency decision. A service that starts by default is a service somebody eventually starts in the wrong place.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport service will not start in a production environment. Its DPIA has not been signed.
refusals.why: The development flag and a production environment together are a contradiction, and the safe reading of a contradiction is no.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport needs a master key of its own in MYTHUSO_PASSPORT_MASTER_KEY: 64 hexadecimal characters, generated for this service alone.
refusals.why: Its own keys are the first of the master document's three boundaries.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport's master key is the identity service's key, or is derived from it. A compromise of one would be a compromise of both, so the Passport will not start.
refusals.why: The design test in §16: with the Core compromised, the attacker has a store they cannot decrypt. That is false the moment the keys are related.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport's database is the identity service's database. The Passport has a store of its own or it does not run.
refusals.why: No other engine holds a copy, and no other engine's file holds this one.

refusals.sentence: The Health Passport answers on the loopback address, to a loopback host name, only. There is no network path to it from anywhere but this machine.
refusals.why: Until the controls exist, the gateway is not a network service at all, and a page in a browser that has rebound a hostname to this machine is not this machine.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the body is not a JSON object this service will read.
refusals.why: A body that cannot be read is refused before anything is decided, and written down like any other refusal.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the Passport has no such route.
refusals.why: A probe for a route that does not exist is still a request somebody made, and the chain records it.

refusals.sentence: Refused: creating a synthetic subject needs a developer credential minted at the console. Nothing reaching the loopback creates a patient on its own.
refusals.why: A route that mints a patient session for whoever asks is a patient-minting door held open to every process on the machine and every page a browser was tricked into loading.

refusals.sentence: Refused: there is no consent grant on this request. The Passport opens nothing without a grant, a break-glass justification or the patient's own session.
refusals.why: Deny by default (§19).

refusals.sentence: Refused: this grant was not signed by the Passport, or it has been altered since.
refusals.why: A grant is a signed artefact. One the gateway cannot verify is not a weaker grant, it is no grant.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the patient has revoked this grant.
refusals.why: Revocation propagates immediately (§21).

refusals.sentence: Refused: this grant has expired. Grants expire by default, and a new one has to be asked for.
refusals.why: Grants expire by default (§21).

refusals.sentence: Refused: this grant would last longer than a grant to this role may. Ask again with an earlier end date.
refusals.why: Each role's maxExpiryDays in packages/catalog/consent.json is a ceiling the patient's choice sits under, and above every role sits the founder's contract-wide grants.maximumExpiryDays, so a grant nobody reviews cannot outlive a quarter.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this grant is for a different person's record.
refusals.why: A grant is one subject's decision about their own record.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the purpose of this request is not the purpose the patient granted.
refusals.why: Purpose of use is on every request, and the grant is for one purpose.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a grant to this role cannot be made for that purpose.
refusals.why: Each role's allowedPurposes in packages/catalog/consent.json are purposes from the gate's own list. A grant for a purpose the role has no reason to hold is a grant for a reason nobody can check.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this category of record is not in the scope the patient granted.
refusals.why: Who × what × why × how long. The what is the scope.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a scheme receives aggregate figures only. No grant opens an identifiable record to a scheme, an insurer or an employer.
refusals.why: The master document states it as a limit on the patient's own power: no such grant type exists (§17).

refusals.sentence: Refused: a responder on a trip reads the emergency summary and the trip's own transport, and nothing else.
refusals.why: §21: emergency summary and mobility note during a trip only.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a care coordinator sees tasks, appointments and summaries, not clinical detail.
refusals.why: §21: a care coordinator's default read excludes clinical detail.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this role can never be given a sealed category, whoever asks.
refusals.why: §21: pharmacists, care coordinators, responders and schemes have no sealed access at all.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the sealed tick has to name the sealed category it opens. A tick with no sealed category in the scope is not accepted.
refusals.why: A tick on its own is a switch, and a switch opens whatever is behind it — including an entry the patient marked private in an ordinary category. The tick opens the sealed categories the scope names, and nothing else.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a sealed category is in this scope without the sealed tick. A sealed category opens only when the patient ticks it in.
refusals.why: Refusing it at the door is clearer than accepting a grant that will silently open nothing of what it names.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that is not a role a grant can name.
refusals.why: A grant to a role the gateway has no rules for is a grant with no rules.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that is not a record category the Passport knows.
refusals.why: Categories are packages/catalog/records.json's, so a scope is never a free-text promise.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this kind of resource cannot be filed under that category.
refusals.why: A category decides who may read an entry. Filing a reading somewhere it does not belong is how it reaches somebody it should not.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the Passport does not accept this kind of resource from a caller.
refusals.why: P0 stores a minimal set, and provenance and audit are written by the gateway alone.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this entry carries something that says who a person is — a name, a phone number, an identity number, an address, an email address or a date of birth. The Passport knows people by a token.
refusals.why: The SA identity number is never a database key or a URL parameter (§19), the identity service already holds who a person is, and a name nested three levels down in an extension is still a name.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a subject is an opaque token the Passport issued, never an identity number or a name.
refusals.why: Tokenised internal ids (§19).

refusals.sentence: Refused: nothing is written into the Passport without provenance — the activity and the system it came from.
refusals.why: Provenance on every write (§20). The author is taken from the request's grant or session, never from the body.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this grant reads and does not write.
refusals.why: §21 gives writes to the patient, the assigned nurse and doctor, and the pharmacist; everybody else reads.

refusals.sentence: Refused: only the patient's own session can do this.
refusals.why: Grants, revocations and the audit log belong to the patient (§26).

refusals.sentence: Refused: this session has ended or expired. Sign in again.
refusals.why: A bearer token that never expires and cannot be ended is a key to a record that outlives the reason it was handed out.

refusals.sentence: Refused: only a registered clinician or the dispatch desk, holding an operator credential, may break the glass.
refusals.why: §21 names the two, and who is asking comes from a credential rather than from what the request says about itself.

refusals.sentence: Refused: breaking the glass needs one of the listed reasons and a note in words, written before anything is opened.
refusals.why: §21: by entering a justification. A reason from a list is what the review can count; the note is what it reads.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the note carries something that looks like a phone number, an identity number or an email address. Say why the glass was broken, not who the patient is.
refusals.why: The note is kept for the review. Who the patient is, the Passport already knows by a token.

refusals.sentence: There is no such record that this request may open.
refusals.why: One sentence for missing and for not yours, so that a refusal does not confirm that somebody else's entry exists.

refusals.sentence: Refused: no share link is made for a scheme, an insurer or an employer. They receive aggregate figures, and a link would hand one of them a person's record.
refusals.why: The identifiable grant to a payer does not exist (§17), and a link is a grant made narrower, never a way round one. Asked before any grant is looked at, so the refusal says nothing about which grants a patient holds.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a share link is for the person the grant it rides on was made to, and this one names somebody else.
refusals.why: A link that could name a different recipient from its grant would be a grant to that recipient that the patient never made.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that is not a kind of link the Passport makes.
refusals.why: The kinds are packages/catalog/passport-sharing.json's, so a link's lifetime and uses always come from a setting somebody can read.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a share link opens no more than the grant it rides on — no category the grant does not name, and nothing sealed the grant did not tick in.
refusals.why: A link is the grant made narrower. A link wider than its grant is a grant nobody signed.

refusals.sentence: Refused: an emergency card opens the emergency summary and nothing else, and never a sealed category.
refusals.why: The card is shown to strangers in an emergency. It carries what a stranger needs to keep somebody safe and nothing a stranger could use against them.

refusals.sentence: Refused: no share link lasts longer than a consent grant may, whatever end date is asked for.
refusals.why: The founder's ceiling in packages/catalog/consent.json holds for every grant, and a link is never longer than the kind of thing it rides on.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this link would last longer than a link of its kind may last today. Ask again with an earlier end date.
refusals.why: How long a link lasts is an admin setting in force when the link is made. Asking past it is refused rather than quietly shortened, so the patient knows the end they get.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a share link ends when the grant it rides on ends, or sooner.
refusals.why: A link that outlived its grant would keep a door open after the patient's decision about it had run out.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this link was not made by the Passport, or it has been altered.
refusals.why: One sentence for a secret that was never issued and one that was changed, so that a guess learns nothing about which links exist.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the patient has revoked this link.
refusals.why: Revocation takes effect at the next use, with no grace, as a grant's does (§21).

refusals.sentence: Refused: this link has ended. Links end by default, and a new one has to be asked for.
refusals.why: Every link ends. A link asked to end in the past is refused in the same words, because it would never have opened.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this link has been opened as many times as it may be. A new one has to be asked for.
refusals.why: A link opened more often than its uses has probably been forwarded, and the patient decided how many times it would open when it was made.

refusals.sentence: Refused: opening a link needs an idempotency key, so that a retry on a bad connection is the same use rather than a second one.
refusals.why: A use counts against a link. A clinic on a dropped connection must not use up a patient's link by retrying.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the Passport exports a FHIR R4 bundle and nothing else yet. An IPS document and a PDF are not built.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/passport-sharing.json lists the formats and which are built. A format answered with something else would be a file that is not what it says.

refusals.sentence: Refused: in development an HL7 message, and the list of messages the Passport could not file, need a developer credential minted at the console. No hospital or laboratory system reaches the Passport.
refusals.why: The door with mutual TLS per partner does not exist (packages/catalog/apis/record.json, doorsToAdd). Until it does, nothing on the loopback sends a message into somebody's record on its own.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this is not an HL7 version 2 message the Passport reads. It has no readable MSH segment, or it lacks a segment or a field its message type needs.
refusals.why: A message read by guessing at its structure is a message filed by guessing. The parser reads the segments packages/catalog/hl7v2-inbound.json names, and refuses the rest.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the message says it is production data. The Passport takes development and training messages on synthetic data only, never one marked for production.
refusals.why: MSH-11 is the partner's own statement of what the data is. A development Passport that accepted a message its sender calls production would be holding a real person's record without its DPIA.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this message's sending application and facility are not a development partner registered with the Passport.
refusals.why: A partner is a responsible party with an agreement and, one day, a certificate. A sender nobody registered is a stranger writing into somebody's record.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this is not a kind of message the Passport reads from this facility.
refusals.why: Each facility is registered for the messages it sends, and each message type says whether it is built. A laboratory sending an admission, or a hospital sending an update the Passport does not read, is refused rather than filed somewhere nearby.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this facility has already sent a different message under this control ID. The same ID twice is the same message once, so a different message needs an ID of its own.
refusals.why: A retry of the same message is answered with its first acknowledgement. A different message under a used ID is either a partner's bug or a message dressed as a retry, and answering it with the first acknowledgement would tell the partner something was filed that was not.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the time this message says it was sent is missing its offset, or is further from the Passport's clock than a message may be, so it cannot be told apart from one replayed or held back.
refusals.why: An instant without an offset is a claim about a timezone nobody stated. How far a partner's clock may drift is an admin setting, read when the message arrives.

refusals.sentence: Refused and quarantined: no patient has linked an identifier in this message, under an authority this facility may use. The message was matched to nobody, and the Passport never matches on a name or a date of birth.
refusals.why: A result filed against the wrong patient is two clinical errors at once. The only match the Passport makes is on a number the patient said is theirs, and a message it cannot match is recorded in the quarantine with nothing it said.

refusals.sentence: Refused: the patient segment carries more than the patient's identifier — a name, a date of birth, an address, a phone number or another field the Passport has no consent basis to store. Nothing from this message was stored.
refusals.why: Who a person is lives in the identity service. A partner that sends it anyway is told so in the acknowledgement, and the patient sees in their own log that it did.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this result names no lab order placed for this patient. A result for an order nobody placed is not filed.
refusals.why: A result with no order behind it has no clinician responsible for acknowledging it, and a result for somebody else's order is the wrong patient's result.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this laboratory is registered to send messages, and no lab order is served by it. A result from a laboratory nobody contracted is not filed.
refusals.why: Whether a laboratory is contracted is Medicines' rule: packages/catalog/medicines.json names which laboratory serves each collection mode, and the lab-result door refuses a laboratory that serves none.

refusals.sentence: Refused: this result names nobody who verified it before it was released. A result with nobody behind it is not filed.
refusals.why: The lab-result door's own condition (packages/catalog/feeds.json, a-result-names-who-verified-it): the question is always asked about the result that was wrong, and somebody has to be there to answer it.

refusals.sentence: Refused: a value in this message looks like a phone number, an identity number or an email address. Nothing from this message was stored.
refusals.why: The same screen every write to the Passport passes. A result is not a place for who somebody is, and a partner that put it there is told so rather than having it filed.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that is not an assigning authority a registered development partner uses.
refusals.why: A number under an authority no partner uses would match no message, and a link that can never match anything is a number kept for no reason.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that number is not shaped like a number this authority issues.
refusals.why: The shape is packages/catalog/hl7v2-inbound.json's. A number typed into the wrong field is refused rather than linked, because a link is what a message is matched on.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that looks like a South African identity number. The Passport never finds a record by one.
refusals.why: The SA identity number is never a database key (§19). It encodes a date of birth and a sex, and it joins every system that has ever stored it.

refusals.sentence: Refused: that number is already linked to a record. A hospital number belongs to one person, so ask the hospital which number is yours.
refusals.why: Two people claiming one number is a mistake or an attempt to receive somebody else's results. The patient it is linked to sees in their own log that somebody tried.
